Tighter money ended the long postwar boom. The Federal Reserve, trying to cool an economy that had been running hot for years, pulled credit back just as the Suez crisis cut off Middle Eastern oil and rattled markets further. What followed felt less like a crash than a slow leak — a grinding decline that stretched across more than a year and pulled the economy into a recession. For a generation of investors who had known almost nothing but rising prices, it was an early reminder that markets can go down and stay down for a while.

The Kennedy-era bull market peaked, slid hard, and turned into one of the sharpest peacetime declines of the century. A sudden one-day plunge that spring — still remembered as the Flash — shook confidence, and the confrontation with the Soviet Union over missiles in Cuba that autumn brought the world to the edge of nuclear war. The mood of those years mixed Cold War dread with frustration at a market that seemed to have lost its footing, and the recovery, when it finally came, felt slow and fragile.

This bear arrived quietly, with no crash at all — the press dubbed it the invisible bear. War spending in Vietnam without matching taxes stoked inflation, and the Federal Reserve answered with a credit crunch that made borrowing expensive and touched off a crisis in the municipal bond market. It was a new kind of bear market, caused not by panic but by deliberate policy tightening, and it taught investors that even a strong economy can produce a nasty decline when credit is withdrawn.

The market topped just as the social and political turbulence of the sixties peaked, and the slide that followed felt endless. The collapse of the Penn Central railroad — the largest corporate failure of its time — froze the commercial paper market and rattled confidence in corporate credit, while inflation kept climbing and the economy sank into recession. A mid-decline rally gave investors hope and then took it away with fresh lows. By the trough, the speculative mutual-fund culture of the decade had been wiped out.

This is the bear that scarred a generation. The oil embargo that followed the Yom Kippur war sent energy prices soaring, inflation surged into double digits, and the Watergate scandal consumed Washington while a president resigned in disgrace. Every rally failed, and the market fell for nearly two years with almost no relief; brokerage houses slashed staff and millions of small investors walked away from stocks. It burned into the national memory the idea that stocks could stay deeply underwater for years, and the recovery, when it finally came, was so widely distrusted that many investors missed it entirely.

The last bear of the great inflation era was caused by the cure rather than the disease. Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve pushed interest rates to extraordinary heights to break inflation's back, and the medicine tipped the economy into a punishing double-dip recession. Borrowing costs for businesses and homebuyers were so high that investment nearly stopped, and stocks ground down through the recession's second dip. Investors endured it knowing, or at least hoping, that the fever was finally breaking.

The most famous single day in market history closed out an otherwise exuberant decade. New portfolio-insurance programs were supposed to protect institutions by selling stock-index futures as prices fell, but when the selling began, the programs fed on themselves and turned a slide into an avalanche on Black Monday. The Dow suffered its worst single session ever, leaving a lasting fear of mechanical, self-reinforcing selling. Yet the economy never tipped into recession, and the market found its footing within months — a lesson in both how terrifying and how resilient the modern market can be.

The dot-com mania took the market to valuations with no historical precedent, and the unwind was every bit as dramatic as the boom. Telecommunications and internet companies that had never earned a profit collapsed, the economy tipped into recession, and the September attacks on New York and Washington closed the exchange and shook the country to its core. Accounting scandals at Enron and WorldCom — names that had been market darlings — then revealed that some of the era's profits had been fiction. For investors it was a slow-motion bear: years of grinding declines and failed rallies, with the uncomfortable discovery that respectable blue-chip companies had fallen nearly as far as the speculative favorites.

The most terrifying bear of the modern era began in the housing market. A nationwide real estate bubble, financed by securitized mortgages of steadily deteriorating quality and held on balance sheets leveraged to the hilt, began to crack, and the losses metastasized through the global banking system. The failure of Lehman Brothers turned a bad market into a full panic — credit froze, and the financial system came closer to collapse than at any time since the Depression. Investors who believed diversification would protect them watched nearly everything fall together, and at the trough respectable voices argued stocks might not recover for a generation. The recovery that followed rewarded those who held on with one of the strongest decades in market history.

The fastest bear market in recorded history. A novel coronavirus spread around the world, and as countries locked down their economies one after another, investors priced in a sudden stop of nearly all economic activity at once. Circuit breakers tripped repeatedly as the market fell faster than it ever had, erasing years of gains in a matter of weeks. The policy response was equally unprecedented, and the trough came so quickly that the next bull market began almost before the fear had registered.

The pandemic-era boom faded as inflation arrived at a four-decade high. Supply-chain snarls, pandemic stimulus, and strong consumer demand combined to push prices up at a pace nobody of working age had ever experienced, and the Federal Reserve answered with the fastest rate-hiking campaign of the modern era. Rising yields pulled the supports out from under both bonds and stocks at the same time, and the grinding decline stretched through most of the year with repeated rallies that each failed. For the first time in decades the classic balanced portfolio offered no shelter — stocks and bonds fell together, and investors relearned how thoroughly inflation reaches into every corner of a portfolio.
